text: unpopular opinion: your posts aren't growing your X account. your replies are.
small account math: your post reaches your 300 followers. your reply on a 100k account's post reaches theirs. replies are the only free distribution you have.
the problem isn't knowing this. it's writing the 15th good reply of the day. that's where everyone quits.
so i built a chrome extension that drafts the reply inside X's reply box. pick a tone — funny, sarcastic, sincere, one-liner — one click, done.

it's called WittyWing. free for 3 days, 10 replies/day, no card needed.

https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/wittywing/nanmlpbedgfahicpngbhalhjokieoipa

deleted the api key setup screen from my extension. activation doubled.

every onboarding step you remove is worth more than any feature you add.

8 tones. 1 click. 0 dashboards.

the whole product lives inside X's reply box. no separate app, no copy-pasting between tabs.

consistency beats brilliance on X.

one great reply does nothing. twenty decent replies a day, every day, compounds into an audience.

credits that never expire shouldn't be a differentiator.

yet here we are.
manifest v3 service workers die silently. if your extension's background script 'randomly stops working', it isn't random. design for it being killed at any moment.

the difference between 'i should reply more' and actually doing it is about 25 seconds per reply.

i built WittyWing to delete those 25 seconds. link in bio.
market cap of your engagement isn't your follower count, it's how many threads you're actually in. replies put you in more threads.
shipped the extension, then spent longer on the store listing than the code. chrome web store review is its own product.
the fastest way to kill a good tool: make people configure it before they can feel the benefit. cut setup, let them feel it first.
most people optimize the tweet. almost nobody optimizes the reply. the reply is read by someone who's already paying attention.
pricing lesson: don't charge for the trial before there's a habit. charge once the habit exists.
link in bio if you want to see what i built for this. otherwise: go reply to three posts today before you write one.
8 tones sounds like a lot until you're mid-argument in someone's replies and need 'sincere' instead of 'sarcastic' in the next 10 seconds. that's the actual use case for WittyWing.
the reply box has less competition than the post composer. everyone's optimizing their next post, almost nobody's optimizing the thing they type into someone else's replies at 11pm tired.
you can tell a founder is early because they still write every reply from scratch. by month six they've either quit replying or built a system for it. there's no third option.
spent a weekend on tone presets for an extension nobody asked for yet. shipped anyway. the only way to find out if 8 tones is the right number or 3 is the right number is to let people pick.
the extensions that survive are the ones that disappear into a workflow you already have. the ones that die ask you to open a new tab first.
free trial math nobody does: 10 replies a day for 3 days is 30 tries to feel a habit. fewer than that and people churn before the thing even clicked.

chrome web store rejected my first submission for a permissions issue i didn't know existed. read the manifest v3 docs twice, still missed it. the review queue teaches you things your code editor won't.
wittywing's whole bet: the reply box is real estate you're already standing in. no dashboard to open, no tab to switch to, just a tone picker where your cursor already is. link in bio.
growth hacking advice for x is mostly about the post. nobody tells you the reply box compounds faster because you're borrowing someone else's audience for free, every time.
wrote replies from scratch for two years before admitting it doesn't scale past a dozen a day. the ones who show up consistently in comments have some system, even a dumb one.
building a chrome extension means your actual competitor isn't another startup, it's chrome's own permission dialog scaring off half your installs before they see the product.
the annoying part of shipping solo: the thing that takes the longest is never the feature, it's the fifty small decisions around it nobody warns you about.
credits that expire are a tax on forgetting. credits that never expire are a bet that people come back when they actually need it, not on your billing cycle.
link in bio if you're curious what a reply-first workflow looks like. the short version: stop opening a blank box and staring at it for a minute per reply.

picked 8 tones instead of 3 because 'friendly' and 'sincere' read completely different mid-thread, and a wrong tone reads worse than no reply at all. https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/wittywing/nanmlpbedgfahicpngbhalhjokieoipa
